claim: WNK1 is a member of a family of four mammalian serine/threonine-specific protein kinases that are broadly conserved across evolution and are found in all multicellular organisms.
source: With No Lysine kinase 1 (WNK1) is a member of a family of four mammalian serine/threonine-specific protein kinases that are broadly conserved across evolution and are found in all multicellular organisms (Veríssimo and Jordan, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Veríssimo and Jordan, 2001.

claim: Mutations in WNK1 and WNK4 result in familial hypertension due to altered salt reabsorption in the kidney.
source: Mutations in WNK1 and WNK4 result in familial hypertension due to altered salt reabsorption in the kidney, because they regulate ion transport in kidney epithelial cells (Wilson et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2001.

claim: WNK kinases phosphorylate and activate the related OXSR1 and STK39 kinases.
source: WNK kinases phosphorylate and activate the related OXSR1 and STK39 kinases, which in turn phosphorylate and activate the Na+K+Cl- co-transporters SLC12A1 and SLC12A2 and the Na+Cl- co-transporter SLC12A3 (Rafiqi et al., 2010; Thastrup et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2010 and Thastrup et al., 2012.

claim: OXSR1 and STK39 kinases phosphorylate and activate the Na+K+Cl- co-transporters SLC12A1 and SLC12A2 and the Na+Cl- co-transporter SLC12A3.
source: WNK kinases phosphorylate and activate the related OXSR1 and STK39 kinases, which in turn phosphorylate and activate the Na+K+Cl- co-transporters SLC12A1 and SLC12A2 and the Na+Cl- co-transporter SLC12A3 (Rafiqi et al., 2010; Thastrup et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rafiqi et al., 2010 and Thastrup et al., 2012.

claim: WNK kinases phosphorylate and inhibit the K+Cl- co-transporters SLC12A4, SLC12A5, SLC12A6, SLC12A7.
source: Furthermore, they phosphorylate and inhibit the K+Cl- co-transporters SLC12A4, SLC12A5, SLC12A6, SLC12A7 (Mercado et al., 2016), blocking K+ and Cl- from leaving the cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mercado et al., 2016.

claim: The net effect of WNK kinase signaling is to promote movement of Na+, K+, and Cl- ions into the cell.
source: Thus, the net effect of WNK kinase signaling is to promote movement of Na+, K+, and Cl- ions into the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the described phosphorylation activities of WNK kinases on ion co-transporters.

claim: WNK1 has been proposed to regulate vesicular trafficking, proliferation and cell volume.
source: Beyond its role in ion homeostasis, WNK1 has been proposed to regulate vesicular trafficking, proliferation and cell volume (de Los Heros et al., 2018; McCormick and Ellison, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to de Los Heros et al., 2018 and McCormick and Ellison, 2011.

claim: Signaling from both the T-cell antigen receptor (TCR) and from the CCR7 chemokine receptor in CD4+ T cells lead to activation of WNK1.
source: Unexpectedly, we recently showed that signaling from both the T-cell antigen receptor (TCR) and from the CCR7 chemokine receptor in CD4+ T cells lead to activation of WNK1 (Köchl et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Köchl et al., 2016.

claim: WNK1 is a negative regulator of TCR- or CCR7-induced adhesion to ICAM1 mediated by LFA1.
source: Furthermore, we found that WNK1 is a negative regulator of TCR- or CCR7-induced adhesion to ICAM1 mediated by LFA1.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous findings as referenced in the text.

claim: WNK1 is a positive regulator of chemokine-induced migration through OXSR1, STK39, and SLC12A2.
source: Conversely, WNK1 is a positive regulator of chemokine-induced migration through OXSR1, STK39, and SLC12A2.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous findings as referenced in the text.

claim: WNK1-deficient T cells home less efficiently to lymphoid organs and migrate more slowly through them.
source: As a result, WNK1-deficient T cells home less efficiently to lymphoid organs and migrate more slowly through them.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous findings as referenced in the text.

claim: Wnk1 expression levels are particularly high in the thymus.
source: Wnk1 expression levels are particularly high in the thymus (Shekarabi et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shekarabi et al., 2013.

claim: The most immature double negative (DN) thymocytes can be subdivided into DN1 (CD25-CD44+CD117+, early thymic progenitors, ETP), DN2 (CD25+CD44+CD117+), DN3 (CD25+CD44-CD117-) and DN4 (CD25-CD44-CD117-) subsets.
source: The most immature double negative (DN) thymocytes, expressing neither CD4 nor CD8, can be subdivided into DN1 (CD25-CD44+CD117+, early thymic progenitors, ETP), DN2 (CD25+CD44+CD117+), DN3 (CD25+CD44-CD117-) and DN4 (CD25-CD44-CD117-) subsets (Bhandoola et al., 2007; Godfrey et al., 1993; Yui et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhandoola et al., 2007; Godfrey et al., 1993; Yui et al., 2010.

claim: DN thymocytes upregulate CD8 and then CD4, becoming CD4-CD8+immature single positive (ISP) cells and then CD4+CD8+double positive (DP) thymocytes.
source: Subsequently, the cells upregulate CD8 and then CD4, becoming CD4-CD8+immature single positive (ISP) cells and then CD4+CD8+double positive (DP) thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of thymocyte development.

claim: DP thymocytes lose expression of either CD4 or CD8 to become CD4+ or CD8+ single positive (4SP or 8SP) cells and emigrate from the thymus as CD4+ or CD8+ T cells.
source: Finally, they lose expression of either CD4 or CD8 to become CD4+ or CD8+ single positive (4SP or 8SP) cells and emigrate from the thymus as CD4+ or CD8+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of thymocyte development.

claim: Thymocytes need to pass three checkpoints to generate T cells that have successfully rearranged both TCRα and TCRβ genes and express an αβTCR that is both restricted by self-MHC and self-tolerant.
source: To generate T cells that have successfully rearranged both TCRα and TCRβ genes and express an αβTCR that is both restricted by self-MHC and self-tolerant, thymocytes need to pass three checkpoints (Carpenter and Bosselut, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carpenter and Bosselut, 2010.

claim: Thymic progenitors migrate from the bone marrow via the blood, entering the thymus at the cortico-medullary junction as DN1 cells (ETP).
source: Thymic progenitors migrate from the bone marrow via the blood, entering the thymus at the cortico-medullary junction as DN1 cells (ETP).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of thymocyte development.

claim: DN2 and DN3 thymocytes begin to re-arrange TCRβ genes and migrate to the sub-capsular zone of the cortex.
source: DN2 and DN3 thymocytes begin to re-arrange TCRβ genes and migrate to the sub-capsular zone of the cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of thymocyte development.

claim: If TCRβ rearrangement is successful, TCRβ protein binds to pre-Tα and together with CD3γ, CD3δ, CD3ε and CD3ζ forms the pre-TCR.
source: If rearrangement is successful, TCRβ protein binds to pre-Tα and together with CD3γ, CD3δ, CD3ε and CD3ζ forms the pre-TCR (Yamasaki and Saito, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamasaki and Saito, 2007.

claim: Signals from the pre-TCR within DN3 cells result in an increase in cell size and expression of CD27 and CD28.
source: Signals from the pre-TCR within DN3 cells result in an increase in cell size and expression of CD27 andCD28, changes which can be used to distinguish DN3a and DN3b cells before and after pre-TCR signaling respectively (Hoffman et al., 1996; Taghon et al., 2006; Teague et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoffman et al., 1996; Taghon et al., 2006; Teague et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2005.

claim: Pre-TCR signals are required for the survival and proliferative expansion of DN3b and DN4 thymocytes, and subsequent differentiation into ISP and DP cells, a checkpoint termed β-selection.
source: Pre-TCR signals are required for the survival and proliferative expansion of DN3b and DN4 thymocytes, and subsequent differentiation into ISP and DP cells, a checkpoint termed β-selection (Kreslavsky et al., 2012; Mingueneau et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kreslavsky et al., 2012; Mingueneau et al., 2013.

claim: Progression through the β-selection checkpoint is supported by signals from CXCR4 and NOTCH1.
source: Progression through this checkpoint is also supported by signals from CXCR4 and NOTCH1 (Janas et al., 2010; Maillard et al., 2006; Trampont et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Janas et al., 2010; Maillard et al., 2006; Trampont et al., 2010.

claim: DP thymocytes rearrange TCRα genes in the cortex.
source: Subsequently, DP thymocytes, now in the cortex, rearrange TCRα genes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of thymocyte development.

claim: If DP thymocytes successfully make an αβTCR that can bind weakly to self-peptide-MHC complexes, the cells undergo positive selection into 4SP and 8SP cells and migrate into the medulla.
source: If they successfully make an αβTCR that can bind weakly to self-peptide-MHC complexes, the cells undergo positive selection into 4SP and 8SP cells and migrate into the medulla (Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klein et al., 2014.

claim: If the αβTCR binds strongly to self-peptide-MHC, auto-reactive T cells are eliminated by negative selection.
source: Alternatively, if the αβTCR binds strongly to self-peptide-MHC, auto-reactive T cells are eliminated by negative selection.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of thymocyte development.

claim: Wnk1 is the only member of the WNK-family expressed in thymocytes, with high expression at all stages of development.
source: We found that Wnk1 is the only member of the WNK-family expressed in thymocytes, with high expression at all stages of development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substantially more Oxsr1 than Stk39 is expressed at all stages of thymocyte development, except for 4SP thymocytes where the expression of Stk39 exceeds levels of Oxsr1.
source: Substantially more Oxsr1 than Stk39 is expressed at all stages, except for 4SP thymocytes where the expression of Stk39 exceeds levels of Oxsr1.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Of the Na+K+Cl- and Na+Cl- co-transporters, only Slc12a2 is expressed in the thymus.
source: Of the Na+K+Cl- and Na+Cl- co-transporters, only Slc12a2 is expressed in the thymus.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is substantial expression of the Slc12a6 and Slc12a7 K+Cl- co-transporters in the thymus.
source: Finally, there is substantial expression of the Slc12a6 and Slc12a7 K+Cl- co-transporters.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of WNK1 resulted in a 10-fold reduction in total thymocyte numbers.
source: We found that loss of WNK1 resulted in a 10-fold reduction in total thymocyte numbers and a progressive loss of cells from the DN4 stage onwards, with a 92% reduction in numbers of ISP thymocytes and a 98–99% reduction in DP, 4SP, and 8SP thymocytes (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C comparing Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice with control Wnk1fl/+CD2-Cre mice.

claim: Loss of WNK1 resulted in a 92% reduction in numbers of ISP thymocytes.
source: We found that loss of WNK1 resulted in a 10-fold reduction in total thymocyte numbers and a progressive loss of cells from the DN4 stage onwards, with a 92% reduction in numbers of ISP thymocytes and a 98–99% reduction in DP, 4SP, and 8SP thymocytes (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C comparing Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice with control Wnk1fl/+CD2-Cre mice.

claim: Loss of WNK1 resulted in a 98–99% reduction in DP, 4SP, and 8SP thymocytes.
source: We found that loss of WNK1 resulted in a 10-fold reduction in total thymocyte numbers and a progressive loss of cells from the DN4 stage onwards, with a 92% reduction in numbers of ISP thymocytes and a 98–99% reduction in DP, 4SP, and 8SP thymocytes (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C comparing Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice with control Wnk1fl/+CD2-Cre mice.

claim: Loss of WNK1 resulted in no change in the numbers of TCRγδ+ thymocytes.
source: In contrast, there was no change in the numbers of TCRγδ+ thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice with control Wnk1fl/+CD2-Cre mice.

claim: Wnk1 expression was lost in DN and ISP populations in thymi from Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice.
source: Analysis of Wnk1 mRNA levels showed that while Wnk1 expression was lost in DN and ISP populations in thymi from Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice, from the DP stage onwards the expression levels were similar to or higher in comparison to control animals (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: From the DP stage onwards in Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice, Wnk1 expression levels were similar to or higher in comparison to control animals, demonstrating that the few remaining DP cells are those that have failed to delete Wnk1.
source: Analysis of Wnk1 mRNA levels showed that while Wnk1 expression was lost in DN and ISP populations in thymi from Wnk1fl/flCD2-Cre mice, from the DP stage onwards the expression levels were similar to or higher in comparison to control animals (Figure 1D), demonstrating that the few remaining DP cells are those that have failed to delete Wnk1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: WNK1 is absolutely required for the development of DP thymocytes.
source: Hence, WNK1 is absolutely required for the development of DP thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing loss of DP thymocytes in WNK1-deficient mice.

claim: Development of thymocytes expressing only WNK1-D368A was very strongly blocked from the DN4 stage onwards.
source: We found that after 7d of tamoxifen treatment, development of thymocytes expressing only WNK1-D368A was again very strongly blocked from the DN4 stage onwards (Figure 1E,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radiation chimeras shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: WNK1 kinase activity is required for thymocyte development from the DN to DP stages.
source: demonstrating that WNK1 kinase activity is required for thymocyte development from the DN to DP stages.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that kinase-inactive WNK1-D368A cannot support thymocyte development.

claim: Loss of WNK1 results in no change in the number of DN3a cells, but a substantial drop in DN3b and DN4 cells.
source: Loss of WNK1 results in no change in the number of DN3a cells, but a substantial drop in DN3b and DN4 cells, consistent with a block at the pre-TCR β-selection checkpoint (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A similar fraction (~10%) of both control and WNK1-deficient DN2 and DN3 thymocytes expressed intracellular TCRβ.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of DN2 and DN3 thymocytes showed that a similar fraction (~10%) of both control and WNK1-deficient cells expressed intracellular TCRβ, corresponding to cells that have successfully rearranged the TCRβ locus, indicating that loss of WNK1 does not impair TCRβ locus rearrangement (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Loss of WNK1 does not impair TCRβ locus rearrangement.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of DN2 and DN3 thymocytes showed that a similar fraction (~10%) of both control and WNK1-deficient cells expressed intracellular TCRβ, corresponding to cells that have successfully rearranged the TCRβ locus, indicating that loss of WNK1 does not impair TCRβ locus rearrangement (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Most control DN4 cells expressed intracellular TCRβ, whereas only ~10% of WNK1-deficient DN4 cells express intracellular TCRβ.
source: A similar analysis of DN4 cells showed that most control cells expressed intracellular TCRβ, as would be expected for cells successfully undergoing β-selection. In contrast, only ~10% of WNK1-deficient DN4 cells express intracellular TCRβ, similar to the percentage in DN3 cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the absence of WNK1, there is no selective expansion of TCRβ+ cells.
source: Thus, in the absence of WNK1, there is no selective expansion of TCRβ+ cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the flow cytometry data showing similar percentages of TCRβ+ cells in DN3 and DN4 populations in WNK1-deficient mice.

claim: Cell-surface levels of CD3ε and pre-Tα in WNK1-deficient DN2 and DN3 cells were comparable to controls.
source: Cell-surface levels of CD3ε and pre-Tα in WNK1-deficient DN2 and DN3 cells were comparable to controls, while CD3ε levels were increased in WNK1-deficient DN4 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CD3ε levels were increased in WNK1-deficient DN4 cells.
source: Cell-surface levels of CD3ε and pre-Tα in WNK1-deficient DN2 and DN3 cells were comparable to controls, while CD3ε levels were increased in WNK1-deficient DN4 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The developmental block in WNK1-deficient DN thymocytes is unlikely to be due to a failure to make pre-TCR subunits.
source: Taken together, these results show that the developmental block in WNK1-deficient DN thymocytes is unlikely to be due to a failure to make pre-TCR subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing normal expression of pre-TCR components in WNK1-deficient cells.

claim: Injection of anti-CD3ε into control Wnk1fl/+Rag1-/-CD2-Cre mice resulted in the generation of large numbers of DP thymocytes.
source: As expected, injection of anti-CD3ε into control Wnk1fl/+Rag1-/-CD2-Cre mice resulted in the generation of large numbers of DP thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DP thymocytes were almost completely absent in anti-CD3ε treated Wnk1fl/flRag1-/-CD2-Cre mice.
source: By stark contrast, DP thymocytes were almost completely absent in anti-CD3ε treated Wnk1fl/flRag1-/-CD2-Cre mice (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: WNK1 is essential for pre-TCR signaling that controls the DN-DP transition in thymocytes.
source: indicating that WNK1 is essential for pre-TCR signaling that controls the DN-DP transition in thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anti-CD3ε injection experiment in RAG1-deficient mice.

claim: The biggest differences between RNAseq samples were caused by anti-CD3ε stimulation and not by genotype.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the results revealed that the biggest differences between the samples were caused by anti-CD3ε stimulation and not by genotype (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both WNK1-deficient thymocytes and control cells followed a similar trajectory on the PCA plot as a function of time after anti-CD3ε injection.
source: Both, WNK1-deficient thymocytes and control cells followed a similar trajectory on the PCA plot as a function of time after anti-CD3ε injection, suggesting that pre-TCR signaling is able to induce similar transcriptional changes in control and WNK1-deficient thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pre-TCR signaling is able to induce similar transcriptional changes in control and WNK1-deficient thymocytes.
source: Both, WNK1-deficient thymocytes and control cells followed a similar trajectory on the PCA plot as a function of time after anti-CD3ε injection, suggesting that pre-TCR signaling is able to induce similar transcriptional changes in control and WNK1-deficient thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from PCA analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: A large number of statistically significant differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified at each time point when comparing control and WNK1-deficient thymocytes, including in unstimulated cells.
source: Nevertheless, comparing the transcriptomes of control and WNK1-deficient thymocytes, we identified a large number of statistically significant differentially expressed genes (DEGs) at each time point, including in unstimulated cells (Figure 3D, Supplementary files 2, 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary files 2, 3.

claim: Most of the identified processes from DEG analysis fit into five functional groups: genes associated with TCR signaling, protein translation, cytoskeleton, adhesion and cell cycle.
source: To further characterize these changes, we carried out a process enrichment analysis taking into account all DEGs at each time point and found that most of the identified processes fit into five functional groups: genes associated with TCR signaling, protein translation, cytoskeleton, adhesion and cell cycle (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by process enrichment analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The TCR signaling and translation signatures were most enriched at the 0 hr time point.
source: The TCR signaling and translation signatures were most enriched at the 0 hr time point, cytoskeleton and adhesion at 48 hr, and cell cycle at 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by process enrichment analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cytoskeleton and adhesion signatures were most enriched at 48 hr.
source: The TCR signaling and translation signatures were most enriched at the 0 hr time point, cytoskeleton and adhesion at 48 hr, and cell cycle at 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by process enrichment analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cell cycle signature was most enriched at 24 hr.
source: The TCR signaling and translation signatures were most enriched at the 0 hr time point, cytoskeleton and adhesion at 48 hr, and cell cycle at 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by process enrichment analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: WNK1-deficient thymocytes had decreased levels of mRNA for Cd3d, Cd3e, Cd3g, Lck, and Syk.
source: Inspection of the TCR signaling signature showed that WNK1-deficient thymocytes had decreased levels of mRNA for Cd3d, Cd3e, Cd3g, Lck, and Syk, coding for CD3 proteins and the LCK and SYK tyrosine kinases and an increase in Lcp2 mRNA, which codes for the SLP76 adapter protein (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: WNK1-deficient thymocytes had an increase in Lcp2 mRNA, which codes for the SLP76 adapter protein.
source: Inspection of the TCR signaling signature showed that WNK1-deficient thymocytes had decreased levels of mRNA for Cd3d, Cd3e, Cd3g, Lck, and Syk, coding for CD3 proteins and the LCK and SYK tyrosine kinases and an increase in Lcp2 mRNA, which codes for the SLP76 adapter protein (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both control and WNK1-deficient cells upregulated Nur77, Cd27, and Cd28, and downregulated Il2ra, Hes1, Rag2, and Ptcra to a similar extent after pre-TCR stimulation.
source: However, analysis of transcriptional changes driven by pre-TCR stimulation showed that both control and WNK1-deficient cells upregulated Nur77, Cd27, and Cd28, and downregulated Il2ra, Hes1, Rag2, and Ptcra to a similar extent (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Anti-CD3ε-induced downregulation of surface levels of CD25 occurred normally in WNK1-deficient cells.
source: Furthermore, anti-CD3ε-induced downregulation of surface levels of CD25 (encoded by Il2ra) also occurred normally in WNK1-deficient cells (Figures 3B and 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3B and 4C.

claim: Loss of WNK1 does not have a major effect on pre-TCR signaling, at least for the first 24 hr after stimulation.
source: These results imply that loss of WNK1 does not have a major effect on pre-TCR signaling, at least for the first 24 hr after stimulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the RNAseq and flow cytometry data showing normal early responses to pre-TCR stimulation.

claim: Many genes in translation processes were downregulated in WNK1-deficient cells, particularly at the 0 hr time point.
source: The most highly enriched processes in the RNAseq analysis were associated with protein translation, with many of the genes in these processes being downregulated in WNK1-deficient cells, particularly at the 0 hr time point (Figure 3E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: pS6 levels in WNK1-deficient cells were similar to those in control cells before stimulation and higher than in controls 24 hr after anti-CD3ε stimulation.
source: We found that pS6 levels in WNK1-deficient cells were similar to those in control cells before stimulation and higher than in controls 24 hr after anti-CD3ε stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rates of protein synthesis were increased to a similar extent by anti-CD3ε in both control and mutant thymocytes.
source: Furthermore, rates of protein synthesis were increased to a similar extent by anti-CD3ε in both control and mutant thymocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein synthesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The absence of WNK1 does not cause substantial changes in rates of protein synthesis.
source: Thus, despite the reduced expression of genes associated with translation, the absence of WNK1 does not cause substantial changes in rates of protein synthesis, and these are unlikely to explain the developmental block.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the protein synthesis assay data.

claim: At the 24 hr time point WNK1-deficient thymocytes had increased expression of Itgb2 and Itgal, the subunits of LFA1.
source: At the 24 hr time point WNK1-deficient thymocytes had increased expression of Itgb2 and Itgal, the subunits of LFA1, as well as Rap1a and Rap2a that encode GTPases required for integrin signaling, and several chemokine receptors (Ccr2, Ccr5, and Cxcr5), although Cxcr4 expression was reduced (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WNK1-deficient thymocytes had increased expression of Rap1a and Rap2a that encode GTPases required for integrin signaling.
source: At the 24 hr time point WNK1-deficient thymocytes had increased expression of Itgb2 and Itgal, the subunits of LFA1, as well as Rap1a and Rap2a that encode GTPases required for integrin signaling, and several chemokine receptors (Ccr2, Ccr5, and Cxcr5), although Cxcr4 expression was reduced (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WNK1-deficient thymocytes had increased expression of several chemokine receptors (Ccr2, Ccr5, and Cxcr5), although Cxcr4 expression was reduced.
source: At the 24 hr time point WNK1-deficient thymocytes had increased expression of Itgb2 and Itgal, the subunits of LFA1, as well as Rap1a and Rap2a that encode GTPases required for integrin signaling, and several chemokine receptors (Ccr2, Ccr5, and Cxcr5), although Cxcr4 expression was reduced (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cell-surface LFA1 was increased on both WNK1-deficient DN2+DN3 and DN4 thymocytes.
source: In agreement with this, cell-surface LFA1 was increased and CXCR4 was decreased on both WNK1-deficient DN2+DN3 and DN4 thymocytes (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CXCR4 was decreased on both WNK1-deficient DN2+DN3 and DN4 thymocytes.
source: In agreement with this, cell-surface LFA1 was increased and CXCR4 was decreased on both WNK1-deficient DN2+DN3 and DN4 thymocytes (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CXCL12 resulted in the phosphorylation of OXSR1 in DN3 thymocytes, which was abrogated in WNK1 inhibitor-treated cells.
source: We found that CXCL12 resulted in the phosphorylation of OXSR1, which was abrogated in WNK1 inhibitor-treated cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CXCR4 transduces signals through WNK1 leading to the phosphorylation and, presumably, activation of OXSR1.
source: Thus, CXCR4 transduces signals through WNK1 leading to the phosphorylation and, presumably, activation of OXSR1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the immunoblotting data showing CXCL12-induced OXSR1 phosphorylation that is WNK1-dependent.

claim: In response to stimulation through either CD3ε or CXCR4, or with Mn2+, WNK1-deficient DN3 thymocytes showed increased binding of ICAM1, indicating increased LFA1-mediated adhesion.
source: We found that in response to stimulation through either CD3ε or CXCR4, or with Mn2+ which directly activates LFA1, WNK1-deficient DN3 thymocytes showed increased binding of ICAM1, indicating increased LFA1-mediated adhesion (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: WNK1-deficient DN3 cells had reduced migration in response to CXCL12.
source: Furthermore, WNK1-deficient DN3 cells had reduced migration in response to CXCL12 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: WNK1 is a negative regulator of LFA1-mediated adhesion in DN3 thymocytes.
source: Thus, WNK1 is a negative regulator of LFA1-mediated adhesion and a positive regulator of CXCL12-induced migration in DN3 thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the adhesion assay data.

claim: WNK1 is a positive regulator of CXCL12-induced migration in DN3 thymocytes.
source: Thus, WNK1 is a negative regulator of LFA1-mediated adhesion and a positive regulator of CXCL12-induced migration in DN3 thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the migration assay data.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Onoyama et al., 2007.

claim: Loss of both OXSR1 and STK39 leads to a block at the pre-TCR checkpoint, along with reduced MYC levels and decreased proliferation of DN4 thymocytes.
source: Since loss of both OXSR1 and STK39 also leads to a block at the pre-TCR checkpoint, along with reduced MYC levels and decreased proliferation of DN4 thymocytes, we hypothesize that WNK1 transduces pre-TCR and CXCR4 signals via OXSR1 and STK39 to the upregulation of MYC, and hence to entry into S-phase and increased cell division.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from OXSR1/STK39 double mutant mice.

claim: WNK1 transduces pre-TCR and CXCR4 signals via OXSR1 and STK39 to the upregulation of MYC, and hence to entry into S-phase and increased cell division.
source: Since loss of both OXSR1 and STK39 also leads to a block at the pre-TCR checkpoint, along with reduced MYC levels and decreased proliferation of DN4 thymocytes, we hypothesize that WNK1 transduces pre-TCR and CXCR4 signals via OXSR1 and STK39 to the upregulation of MYC, and hence to entry into S-phase and increased cell division.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the combined data from WNK1, OXSR1, and STK39 mutant mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by the data from SLC12A2-deficient chimeras.

claim: Among >1400 cancer cell lines, the expression of WNK1 is highest in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) lines.
source: Interestingly, among >1400 cancer cell lines, the expression of WNK1 is highest in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) lines, many of which originate from immature thymocytes (Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia, CCLE https://portals.broadinstitute.org/ccle) (Barretina et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia and citations to Barretina et al., 2012 and Tan et al., 2017.

claim: T-ALL lines are the most sensitive to loss of WNK1, as measured by growth inhibition.
source: Furthermore, T-ALL lines are the most sensitive to loss of WNK1, as measured by growth inhibition (CCLE) (Tsherniak et al., 2017), implying that WNK1 plays a key role in these thymically-derived tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia and a citation to Tsherniak et al., 2017.

claim: WNK1 plays a key role in T-ALL tumors.
source: Furthermore, T-ALL lines are the most sensitive to loss of WNK1, as measured by growth inhibition (CCLE) (Tsherniak et al., 2017), implying that WNK1 plays a key role in these thymically-derived tumors.

claim: T-ALL cells express high levels of MYC, which is essential for their proliferation.
source: Since T-ALL cells express high levels of MYC, which is essential for their proliferation (Sanchez-Martin and Ferrando, 2017), we hypothesize that WNK1 may contribute to the growth of T-ALL by maintaining high levels of MYC, making WNK1 a potential therapeutic target in this thymocyte-derived leukemia.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sanchez-Martin and Ferrando, 2017.
